cells.tense: You are giving and receiving in the same motion right now, and the scale reads level.
cells.ask: Before the next stretch where neither of you can see the whole road, send one short check-in instead of the long story, and let the reply be enough.
cells.core:
You're giving and taking in the same motion, and you can feel when it's level. What you hand someone comes back, and you let it come back — you don't keep a scoreboard. That's rarer than you'd think. Most people either give past the point of return or take without noticing.

The hard part is you do it in fog. You can't see the whole road ahead, so you feel your way, and the feeling is what keeps the exchange honest. What works now: keep watching what comes back, not just what you send. When it's level, name it, out loud or just to yourself. Staying level is the whole job, not a stop on the way to some louder version of you.
cells.sheetLine: You give and receive in the same motion, and you can tell when it's level.
cells.verb: Passing what is given back and forth until it comes out even
cells.place: In the fog where the next step is visible and the far end is not

cells.tense: You are bracing for a fairness that hasn't arrived yet, and you're already spending against it.
cells.ask: Pick one account you've been running in your head and put the number down where someone else can see it, then stop counting for a day.
cells.core:
You're living one step ahead of the exchange. Before anyone's asked, you've already drafted what you'll give, what you'll get, and how it'll come out even. You're bracing for the fairness like it might not arrive on its own — and the bracing is eating the thing it's about.

Nobody feels generous toward a calculator. What you're holding for is a level that can't be written in advance; it gets set by the two of you, moving. Try one account. Write the number down where it can be seen, then leave it alone for a day. Standing firm here doesn't mean gripping the tally. It means holding your own ground while the count comes out somewhere you didn't plan.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a closed door and sending nothing through it.
cells.ask: Take one small thing offered to you this week without giving anything back — say thank you and let that be the end of it.
cells.core:
You stopped giving because you stopped being able to tell what was fair. The accounting shut down somewhere, and you shut down with it. What's left isn't stinginess. It's that nothing arrives clearly enough now to trust — you can't sort what's genuinely offered from what's expected, so the safest move has been to send nothing out.

What sharpens is attention, not generosity. One thing at a time, until the fog has edges. Solitude helps here; alone, you can tell what's yours and what's theirs without anyone watching. Then the exchange can start again, small. Notice one thing that's genuinely offered to you, and let it land before you think about what you owe back.

cells.tense: You are already trading fairly with people around you, and you talk about it like it's just how things work.
cells.ask: Tell one person a plain thing you feel about the two of you — no preamble, no question attached — and let it sit.
cells.core:
You're already keeping it even. You adjust, you give, you take — and if someone asked, you'd say that's just being decent. But the fairness you're running is yours. You decided, somewhere, what counts and how much, and you've been calling it common sense.

A hunch about what's fair shows up before you can argue for it, and it's right often enough that you act on it without checking twice. What's off now is that you do it silently. You feel the balance between you and someone and say nothing, so the judgment stays invisible, even to you. Say one of those things plainly, without dressing it as a question. What you felt holds up. It just hasn't been claimed.
